First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=3-\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{3-\text{i}}=3+\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(3-\text{i}+(3+\text{i)})x+(3-\text{i})(3+\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+({3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+10 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-6x+10$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x+2 \\  & {x}^{2}-6x+10\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-\phantom{2}2x+20} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+10x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,2{x}^{2}-12x+20 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{2{x}^{2}-12x+20}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

     

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-6x+10)(x+2).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2=0\,⟹\,x=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=-2,3\pm \text{i}.$

First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116.$

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-5+2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-5+2\text{i}}=-5-2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(-5+2\text{i}+(-5-2\text{i)})x+(-5+2\text{i})(-5-2\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+((-5)^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+29 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+10x+29$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x-4 \\  & {x}^{2}+10x+29\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}+\phantom{1}6{x}^{2}-11x-116} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+10{x}^{2}+29x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,-4{x}^{2}+40x-116 \\  & \,\,\,{-4{x}^{2}+40x-116}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

        

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+10x+29)(x-4).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=4,-5\pm 2\text{i}.$

Consider a system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables, written in matrix form as $D\,z=c.$ Here, $D$ is the non-singular coefficient matrix of the system, $z$ is the column vector containing the variables, and $c$ is the column vector containing the constants. The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & =\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{D}^{-1}}}}c \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{I}_{n}}}}z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

From top to bottom and right to left, what are the missing parts of the derivation?

The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,t & =q \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{D}^{-1}}}}D\,t & ={D}^{-1}\,q \\ {I}_{n}\,t & ={D}^{-1}\,\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{\mathbf{q}}}} \\ t & ={D}^{-1}\,q\end{aligned}
$$
